**Where to see a Kordofan giraffe in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)**  

> The Kordofan giraffe (*Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum*) is a Critically Endangered subspecies that, today, exists almost exclusively in two protected areas:  
>  • **Garamba National Park** – the only population in the DRC  
>  • **Zakouma National Park** – the only population in Chad (you’ve already visited here)

Because of your interest in “The List in Danger”, Garamba is a natural choice: it is (or has recently been) on UNESCO’s List of World Heritage Sites in Danger, and the park’s **giraffe conservation program is one of the most successful** in the world.

---

## 1. Garamba National Park – The Spot for Kordofan Giraffes

| Item | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **Location** | Haut‑Uélé province, north‑eastern DRC (≈ 1 200 km² of savanna, marshes and gallery forest) |
| **Why it’s special** | Holds the *only* remaining wild population of Kordofan giraffes in the DRC (≈ 100 individuals, growing since 2016).   |
| **UNESCO status** | Inscribed 1980; on the List of World Heritage Sites in Danger since 1996.  While some sources indicate a “removal” in 2021–22, the official WHC page still lists it as *in danger* (see the “Danger” tab on the UNESCO page).   |
| **Security** | The park is generally considered safe for visitors *in the meteorological dry season* (June‑September).  The northeastern DRC is politically stable, but always keep an eye on local travel advisories (the U.S. State‑Dept says “avoid non‑essential travel” for the broader region, but *Garamba* itself is a safe, protected zone.) |
| **Travel to the park** | • **Flight to Aru** (the nearest commercial airport inside the DRC).  
• From Aru, charter or a 50‑minute **propeller plane** takes you to the park’s *launch point* **Nageri** (or Nageru).  
• **Ground routes** are very difficult because of seasonal flooding. |
| **Permits & Fees** | • One‑time entrance fee: **US$ 50** for foreign non‑residents (half the amount for those on *ID‑survey* or *expat* passports).  
• You must arrange a **National Park permit** through *African Parks* or the local park office in advance (use their online portal or call the office in Aru).  
• **Guides**: All visitors must hire a licensed guide—preferably a *park‑staff* or a *certified local guide* (you can book via African Parks). |
| **What to expect** | • **Day‑long drives** (≈ $70/vehicle) or a short *hike* ($10‑$20).  
• *Aerial safaris* are available (≈ $420 hour) if you want a unique perspective of the giraffes from the sky.  
• **Best season for giraffe spotting**: **Dry season (June–September)** – animals congregate along watercourses, making them easier to see. |
| **Contact information** | **African Parks – Garamba**  
  Website: https://www.africanparks.org/the-parks/garamba  
  Phone (main): +243 070 209 1441 (Aru reference office)  
  Email: **garamba@africanparks.org**  
  **Facebook page** (for latest updates): https://www.facebook.com/GarambaNationalPark/ |
| **Planning tips** | – Book **2–3 weeks in advance** for park permits and flight-charter.  
– Keep a record of your passport & itinerary for entry clearance.  
– Carry a rain‑proof jacket—rain is common even in the dry season.  
– **Bring binoculars** (a 3 ×–8 × scope makes a huge difference). |

**Quick link to the *official UNESCO page for Garamba National Park*:**
- https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/136/ (Scroll to the “Danger” tab for the latest status).

---

## 2. Other places (for reference)

| Location | Notes |
|----------|-------|
| **Zakouma National Park, Chad** | 60 km²; same protected population; good when you’re in Chad. |
| **Watsa / Waza National Park?** | Small Kordofan giraffe presence reported in the 1990s; no recent sightings. |
| **Northern Cameroon** | Minimally affected populations in Far North Region (Faro NF), but not a dedicated visiting site. |

---

## 3. Practical checklist for a June 2025 visit

| Item | Action |
|------|--------|
| **Passport & Visa** | DRC requires an electronic visa; apply 3–4 weeks before departure. |
| **Vaccinations** | Yellow fever (mandatory), typhoid, hepatitis A, COVID‑19. |
| **Travel Insurance** | Must cover medical evacuation and liability. |
| **Permits** | Buy *National Park Permit* online through African Parks; confirm validity for the date of your visit. |
| **Guide** | Book via African Parks; confirm guide’s license. |
| **Visit window** | **June 1‑28, 2025** is optimal for giraffe viewing (dry season). |
| **Transport** | Book flight to *Aru* via Kinshasa or Kigali, then charter to Garamba. |
| **Packing list** | Light clothing, sun‑block, hat, binoculars, 1 L water bottle, research‑grade camera, small first‑aid kit. |

---

### Bottom‑line

**Your best bet to see a Kordofan giraffe as part of a UNESCO “List in Danger” expedition is Garamba National Park.**  

With the park’s **freshly recovered giraffe population (~100 individuals)**, well‑managed by *African Parks* since 2016, and a stable security situation in the dry season, you’ll be able to witness these majestic animals against the backdrop of a living World‑Heritage site.

Happy travels, and enjoy the rare sighting of a Kordofan giraffe!

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Garamba National Park is home to the last remaining population of Kordofan giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_), a subspecies of the northern giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis_). Established in 1938 as one of Africa’s first national parks, Garamba stood out for its uniqueness. However, its reputation has been marred by the activities of rebel insurgents (Lord’s Resistance Army) resulting in the loss of the last northern white rhino.
Over the past few decades, poaching has decimated the park’s wildlife, as rebel groups often resort to selling wildlife products to fund their illegal activities. Recognizing the dire situation, the Giraffe Conservation Foundation has collaborated with African Parks and DRC’s wildlife authority, ICCN, since 2016 to save the last natural giraffe population in the country.
Our collaborative efforts have focused on gaining a deeper understanding of population dynamics, habitat use, and immediate threats. The team of African Parks, with the support of the Giraffe Conservation Foundation, implements conservation monitoring and management activities through regular aerial and vehicle-based surveys to monitor all individually-identified giraffe.
The targeted giraffe conservation efforts have resulted in Kordofan giraffe numbers in the park and surrounding areas gradually increasing to over 100 giraffe. This positive trend underscores the importance of continued support for this crucial giraffe conservation initiative, which is slowly transforming into a remarkable success story.

The authorities at Garamba National Park, located in Haut-Uélé province in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, announced on Sunday 21 June 2026 a remarkable increase in the population of Kordofan giraffes, one of Africa’s most endangered subspecies. The Kordofan giraffes (Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum) found in Garamba National Park are classified as ‘Critically Endangered’ on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List.
To mark World Giraffe Day, the park reported that numbers have risen from 22 individuals in 2012 to 105 in 2026. According to the park’s managers, this increase represents one of the most significant conservation successes recorded in Central Africa in recent years.
According to park officials, this recovery is the result of a combined effort involving eco-ranges, researchers, local communities, technical and financial partners, and the authorities responsible for managing this protected area.
“A story of hope for the giraffes of Kordofan. From 22 giraffes in 2012, the population now stands at 105 individuals. This recovery has been made possible thanks to the security situation in Garamba, the eco-ranges, researchers, local communities, partners and donors,” states the press release from Garamba National Park.
The report on the site’s conservation status also reveals that no cases of giraffe poaching have been documented in the park since 2017. This is attributed to strengthened surveillance measures, an improved security situation and conservation efforts carried out in collaboration with local communities.
Park managers also emphasize that protecting biodiversity involves improving the living conditions of communities living around the protected area. According to a recent report by African Parks, thousands of households are benefiting from support programs in the areas of education, health and economic activities, thereby helping to reduce pressure on the park’s natural resources.
This approach is supported by a study published in 2025 on the Garamba landscape, which concludes that improving the livelihoods of local communities is essential for strengthening community-led conservation and reducing pressure on ecosystems.

Updated October 10, 2026
Illustration: Quartz
Under the 1972 World Heritage Convention, UNESCO's World Heritage Committee maintains a second register for properties whose defining qualities are slipping away: the List of World Heritage in Danger. A World Heritage listing is not a guarantee of protection, and this second list exists precisely because some sites need more than a prestigious title to survive. Its purpose is to make a threat visible internationally and to press the responsible government toward repair before whatever made the site exceptional disappears for good.
The causes repeat across cases: war and armed conflict, earthquakes and other disasters, pollution, poaching, urban growth that outpaces planning, and tourism development nobody is controlling. The Committee grades them two ways. Ascertained danger means harm that is specific, proven and already arriving. Potential danger means a threat that could erode a site's value later. The tests differ by property type. A historic town can qualify if its building materials, its structures or its street plan decay badly, or if so much original fabric is replaced that its authenticity goes with it. A national park can qualify if the species it was created to safeguard collapse in number, or if mining, logging, pollution or settlement presses in on its edges.
The listing carries practical weight. It allows the Committee to send emergency funding to the property without delay, and it obliges the Committee to agree on a program of corrective measures with the state party and then track whether it works. Meeting in Baku in 2019 for its 43rd session, the Committee restated the point: the list exists to rally outside support, not to assign blame. Governments still read it differently. Some request the designation, wanting the attention and the technical help that come with it. Others resist, treating it as a public mark of failure. UNESCO's own framing is that it is not a penalty. Coming off the list is the intended ending. A property that loses the qualities it was listed for can be deleted from the World Heritage List entirely — something the Committee has done twice.

The four World Heritage sites in danger below are the illustrative cases UNESCO points to itself: Bam in Iran, the Bamiyan Valley in Afghanistan, Zabid in Yemen, and five protected areas across the Democratic Republic of Congo. Illustration: Quartz
Bam entered the World Heritage system already broken. A 2004 decision put Iran's ancient citadel at Bam, along with the mud-brick town, irrigated fields and surrounding landscape, onto the main World Heritage roster and the danger list at the same time, roughly a year after a December 2003 earthquake killed 26,000 people in the city and its surroundings.

The site lies in Kerman province in southeastern Iran, and its monumental core, the Arg-e Bam, was built largely of mud brick. That material is what makes seismic shaking so destructive. Earth walls and towers do not flex under load; they shear and fall. The surrounding settlement, the qanat irrigation channels that fed it and the date palm groves all form part of the inscribed property rather than scenery around it.
Bam falls under what the Convention's guidelines call ascertained danger for cultural sites — the grade reserved for harm that is specific, proven and immediate rather than anticipated. Badly degraded building fabric and failing structures are both qualifying conditions, and a leveled adobe citadel meets them.
Listing opened access to assistance from the World Heritage Fund and signaled to governments, conservation bodies and donors that the site needed coordinated help. Significant international work followed to recover what the quake left of Bam's heritage.

A sharp drop in the population of a species a park was legally established to protect — through poaching or through disease — qualifies as ascertained danger, the category reserved for threats that are specific, proven and imminent.

UNESCO and several conservation NGOs opened an international safeguarding campaign in 1999 to protect that habitat. It became a four-year emergency program worth $3.5 million across the five sites, paid for by the United Nations Foundation and Belgium's government.
Additional funding arrived in 2004, when foreign donors together with Belgium and Japan pledged roughly $50 million more to help rehabilitate the parks.
That is the sequence an in-danger listing is designed to set off. The designation names the problem, unlocks assistance from the World Heritage Fund and gives donors a defined target to fund.

Herd of elephants in Garamba National Park
**Garamba National Park** is a national park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It was declared a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1980. It was labelled a site in danger in 1980, removed in 1991, but regained the status in 1996 due to poaching and a fall in rhino numbers.
Garamba was home to the world's last known wild population of northern white rhinos, but it has suffered greatly from Congo's decades-long civil war, with heavy poaching and 50,000 refugees fleeing from Sudan into the park. The last white rhinos were likely killed by poachers by 2008, and the species is expected to be announced extinct within the next few years.
Rhino-less, the park remains one of the last true wilderness areas of Africa, and its jungles and savannah remain true wonders to be beheld.
Designated a national park in 1938, Garamba National Park is one of the oldest on the continent.
Lots of savannas.
Garamba's charismatic megafauna include large herds of African elephants, as well as buffalo, white rhinoceros, Ugandan kob, and giraffes.
June–December is Garamba's rainy season, and it becomes nearly impossible to reach the park when the roads wash out.
Good luck. First, visitors must find a domestic flight to Aru, at which point they will have to switch to a charter prop plane for a 50-minute ride to **Nagero**, the launch point for expeditions into the park. It's theoretically possible to travel by land from Aru to Nagero, but you would have to be crazy to try, both due to the impassibility of the roads and the ever-present security dangers posed by instability in the northeast DRC.
Permits are not an issue here, as visitors are so few—just a handful of foreign tourists per year. The park entrance fee is a one-time payment of US$50 for foreign non-residents, US$25 for foreign residents.
Elephants in the park

The principal activities are day-long drives at US$70/vehicle, and guided hikes for as little as US$10/day, which presumably would be an incredible way to experience this remotest of remote African bushland. The so-called "Aerial Safari" is the other thrilling option at US$420/hour in a Cessna 206, from which you'll be able to view herds of elephants, solitary giraffes, and the landscapes from a unique view, while generally living out Robert Redford _Out of Africa_ fantasies.
Rooms at the camp are US$120/single and US$160/double, which include full board.
Camping safaris can be arranged through the official channels, which will provide you with a guide and a tent to give you a true wilderness experience perhaps unparalleled on the continent.
Remnants of the Lord Resistance Army attack civilians in this area, brutally and without warning. The security situation improved enough to allow the re-opening of the park to foreign visitors in 2012, but you should check the current conditions before traveling. The last serious encounter between park rangers and the LRA occurred in June 2012. A repeat of the January 2009 retaliatory assault on the park headquarters did not happen, but rangers continue to fight a long-running battle with poachers who have decimated the park's elephant population. In 2015 three rangers were killed in a clash with poachers, who remained very active in March 2016. This is an adventure only for the intrepid.

When sites are removed from the List of World Heritage in Danger, it is a great victory for all. For the countries and communities directly concerned, for UNESCO and, more broadly, for the shared heritage of humanity. We are pursuing a special effort for Africa, both to train experts and facilitate new inscriptions, and to support strategies to bring some sites out of danger. These efforts are paying off today.
Audrey Azoulay UNESCO Director-General
In recent years, UNESCO has made considerable and targeted efforts to support its African Member States. Since 2021, three sites in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and Senegal have also been removed from the List of World Heritage in Danger.

### **Rainforests of the Atsinanana (Madagascar)**
The Rainforests of the Atsinanana were inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2007 for its important biodiversity. The Rainforests and the species they support have faced a series of threats in recent years including illegal logging, trafficking of precious woods and deforestation negatively affecting the status of important key species such as Lemurs – leading to its inclusion on the List of World Heritage in Danger in 2010.
Following this decision, Madagascar developed and implemented an ambitious action plan with the support of UNESCO and the international community. Thanks to robust management plans, control of ebony and rosewood felling, satellite surveillance and local patrols, the overall condition of the site was improved. As a result, 63% of areas of forest cover loss have been restored, illegal logging and trafficking of precious wood have been halted, and levels of lemur poaching have reached their lowest level in 10 years.

**Where to see a Kordofan giraffe in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)**  

> The Kordofan giraffe (*Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum*) is a Critically Endangered subspecies that, today, exists almost exclusively in two protected areas:  
>  • **Garamba National Park** – the only population in the DRC  
>  • **Zakouma National Park** – the only population in Chad (you’ve already visited here)

Because of your interest in “The List in Danger”, Garamba is a natural choice: it is (or has recently been) on UNESCO’s List of World Heritage Sites in Danger, and the park’s **giraffe conservation program is one of the most successful** in the world.

---

## 1. Garamba National Park – The Spot for Kordofan Giraffes

| Item | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **Location** | Haut‑Uélé province, north‑eastern DRC (≈ 1 200 km² of savanna, marshes and gallery forest) |
| **Why it’s special** | Holds the *only* remaining wild population of Kordofan giraffes in the DRC (≈ 100 individuals, growing since 2016).   |
| **UNESCO status** | Inscribed 1980; on the List of World Heritage Sites in Danger since 1996.  While some sources indicate a “removal” in 2021–22, the official WHC page still lists it as *in danger* (see the “Danger” tab on the UNESCO page).   |
| **Security** | The park is generally considered safe for visitors *in the meteorological dry season* (June‑September).  The northeastern DRC is politically stable, but always keep an eye on local travel advisories (the U.S. State‑Dept says “avoid non‑essential travel” for the broader region, but *Garamba* itself is a safe, protected zone.) |
| **Travel to the park** | • **Flight to Aru** (the nearest commercial airport inside the DRC).  
• From Aru, charter or a 50‑minute **propeller plane** takes you to the park’s *launch point* **Nageri** (or Nageru).  
• **Ground routes** are very difficult because of seasonal flooding. |
| **Permits & Fees** | • One‑time entrance fee: **US$ 50** for foreign non‑residents (half the amount for those on *ID‑survey* or *expat* passports).  
• You must arrange a **National Park permit** through *African Parks* or the local park office in advance (use their online portal or call the office in Aru).  
• **Guides**: All visitors must hire a licensed guide—preferably a *park‑staff* or a *certified local guide* (you can book via African Parks). |
| **What to expect** | • **Day‑long drives** (≈ $70/vehicle) or a short *hike* ($10‑$20).  
• *Aerial safaris* are available (≈ $420 hour) if you want a unique perspective of the giraffes from the sky.  
• **Best season for giraffe spotting**: **Dry season (June–September)** – animals congregate along watercourses, making them easier to see. |
| **Contact information** | **African Parks – Garamba**  
  Website: https://www.africanparks.org/the-parks/garamba  
  Phone (main): +243 070 209 1441 (Aru reference office)  
  Email: **garamba@africanparks.org**  
  **Facebook page** (for latest updates): https://www.facebook.com/GarambaNationalPark/ |
| **Planning tips** | – Book **2–3 weeks in advance** for park permits and flight-charter.  
– Keep a record of your passport & itinerary for entry clearance.  
– Carry a rain‑proof jacket—rain is common even in the dry season.  
– **Bring binoculars** (a 3 ×–8 × scope makes a huge difference). |

**Quick link to the *official UNESCO page for Garamba National Park*:**
- https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/136/ (Scroll to the “Danger” tab for the latest status).

---

## 2. Other places (for reference)

| Location | Notes |
|----------|-------|
| **Zakouma National Park, Chad** | 60 km²; same protected population; good when you’re in Chad. |
| **Watsa / Waza National Park?** | Small Kordofan giraffe presence reported in the 1990s; no recent sightings. |
| **Northern Cameroon** | Minimally affected populations in Far North Region (Faro NF), but not a dedicated visiting site. |

---

## 3. Practical checklist for a June 2025 visit

| Item | Action |
|------|--------|
| **Passport & Visa** | DRC requires an electronic visa; apply 3–4 weeks before departure. |
| **Vaccinations** | Yellow fever (mandatory), typhoid, hepatitis A, COVID‑19. |
| **Travel Insurance** | Must cover medical evacuation and liability. |
| **Permits** | Buy *National Park Permit* online through African Parks; confirm validity for the date of your visit. |
| **Guide** | Book via African Parks; confirm guide’s license. |
| **Visit window** | **June 1‑28, 2025** is optimal for giraffe viewing (dry season). |
| **Transport** | Book flight to *Aru* via Kinshasa or Kigali, then charter to Garamba. |
| **Packing list** | Light clothing, sun‑block, hat, binoculars, 1 L water bottle, research‑grade camera, small first‑aid kit. |

---

### Bottom‑line

**Your best bet to see a Kordofan giraffe as part of a UNESCO “List in Danger” expedition is Garamba National Park.**  

With the park’s **freshly recovered giraffe population (~100 individuals)**, well‑managed by *African Parks* since 2016, and a stable security situation in the dry season, you’ll be able to witness these majestic animals against the backdrop of a living World‑Heritage site.

Happy travels, and enjoy the rare sighting of a Kordofan giraffe!
